paper.title: Beyond Before-and-After Images: Evaluating Temporal Grounding in a Lightweight VLM for Disaster Assessment
paper.summary: Bi-temporal satellite imagery is central to disaster assessment: deciding what was damaged requires comparing a pre-event scene with its post-event counterpart. A vision-language model (VLM) can nonetheless appear to answer change questions while relying mainly on the post-event image or on the prompt's temporal framing. We present a controlled diagnostic of temporal grounding and apply it to one lightweight VLM, InternVL3-2B, on DisasterM3: 1,659 optical and SAR image pairs from 41 events and nine disaster types, in event-disjoint partitions, with 9,031 reasoning questions. We compare post-only input, the true pre/post pair, the post image repeated twice, reversed image order, and an unrelated pre-event image. The true pair scores $+0.5$ accuracy points above the repeated-post control (95\% paired bootstrap CI $[-0.2, +1.2]$), and reversing the order changes accuracy by $-0.2$ points ($[-0.8, +0.5]$). Under this protocol we therefore find no measurable benefit from the content of the true pre-event image and little sensitivity to temporal order. The model is not blind to the first image, however: the true pair scores $2.5$ points above a pair whose pre-event image comes from another event ($[+1.6, +3.4]$). State-transition and multi-hop questions remain hard, and optical and SAR inputs show different profiles. We outline temporal scene graphs as a testable next step, not a validated solution, and argue that temporal benchmarks for Earth observation should report whether answers depend on the intended evidence, not only how often they are right.
paper.comment: 13 pages (4 main + references + supplementary), 4 figures, 14 tables. Accepted at the CV4EO Workshop, WACV 2027

analysis.problem_statement: The paper investigates whether lightweight Vision-Language Models (VLMs) genuinely utilize pre-event imagery for temporal grounding in disaster assessment or merely rely on post-event images and prompt framing.
analysis.bottleneck_addressed: Lack of verifiable temporal reasoning and evidence attribution in VLMs applied to bi-temporal Earth observation tasks.
analysis.executive_summary: This study provides a controlled diagnostic framework to evaluate if VLMs actually process temporal changes or hallucinate answers based on single-frame cues. It reveals that current lightweight models show negligible sensitivity to the specific content of pre-event images or their temporal order, challenging the assumption that bi-temporal input inherently improves disaster assessment accuracy.

key_metrics.primary_metric: Accuracy difference between true pre/post pairs and repeated-post controls
key_metrics.improvement_percentage: Not quantifiable as a percentage; reported as absolute accuracy points with 95% CI [-0.2, +1.2]

technical_breakdown.method: Controlled diagnostic evaluation using event-disjoint partitions on the DisasterM3 dataset, comparing model performance across five input conditions: post-only, true pre/post, repeated post, reversed order, and unrelated pre-event image.
technical_breakdown.architecture: InternVL3-2B (lightweight VLM) applied to optical and SAR satellite imagery pairs.
technical_breakdown.implementation_details: Utilizes 1,659 image pairs from 41 events and 9,031 reasoning questions. Employs paired bootstrap confidence intervals to assess statistical significance of accuracy differences between control conditions.
technical_breakdown.code_complexity: Evaluation-focused; no new model training described. Computational cost is limited to inference on the specified VLM across the diagnostic test sets.

paper.title: A Face Robot which Imitates Human Musculoskeletal Skin System and Its Evaluation on Basic Movement of Facial Expression
paper.summary: Facial robots require many coordinated, smallamplitude motions, but accommodating these motions in a compact face remains difficult. This paper presents an anatomically inspired facial-robot platform that reproduces the layered organization of the human facial musculoskeletal system. The platform comprises bone, muscle, and skin components whose geometry, shape, and attachment locations are derived from three-dimensional anatomical data. Wire-driven, compliant muscle components are routed through PTFE tubes, allowing actuation to be placed away from the face. We describe the selection and fabrication of 65 muscles (34 muscle types) required to reproduce the 47 target action units (AUs) in the Facial Action Coding System (FACS). We then evaluate the reproducibility of individual AUs in two stages: muscle actuation without skin and actuation after the silicone skin is attached. Forty of the 47 target AUs were reproduced with the muscle components, and 30 were reproduced after skin attachment. These results demonstrate the feasibility of reproducing a broad range of FACS facial expressions using an anatomically inspired musculoskeletal structure. The proposed platform provides a foundation for the systematic development and evaluation of future anatomically inspired facial robots
paper.comment: Accepted to IEEE-RAS Humanoids 2026, website - https://haraduka.github.io/musculoskeletal-face/, youtube - https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=eRuoUJ056uc

analysis.problem_statement: Accommodating the numerous coordinated, small-amplitude motions required for realistic facial expressions within a compact robotic face is difficult due to space and actuation constraints.
analysis.bottleneck_addressed: Hardware actuation density and spatial constraints in embodied AI/robotics, specifically the physical limitation of integrating complex multi-DOF (Degrees of Freedom) mechanisms into compact form factors.
analysis.executive_summary: This work addresses the physical hardware bottleneck in social robotics by providing an anatomically accurate, wire-driven musculoskeletal platform that decouples actuation from the facial structure. It demonstrates the feasibility of reproducing a broad range of FACS expressions (30/47 target AUs with skin) using a systematic, anatomy-derived design, offering a scalable foundation for high-fidelity human-robot interaction.

key_metrics.primary_metric: Reproducibility of Facial Action Coding System (FACS) Action Units (AUs)
key_metrics.metric_value: 30 out of 47 target AUs reproduced with skin attachment; 40 out of 47 without skin
key_metrics.baseline: Implicit baseline of previous compact facial robots which struggle to accommodate coordinated small-amplitude motions; no specific numerical baseline robot is cited in the summary for direct percentage comparison.
key_metrics.improvement_percentage: N/A (Qualitative feasibility demonstration rather than a single percentage improvement over a specific named baseline)

technical_breakdown.method: Anatomically inspired design using 3D anatomical data to derive geometry and attachment locations for bone, muscle, and skin layers. Wire-driven compliant muscles are routed through PTFE tubes to allow off-face actuation.
technical_breakdown.architecture: Layered musculoskeletal system comprising bone, 65 wire-driven muscle components (34 types), and a silicone skin layer. Actuation is externalized to maintain facial compactness.
technical_breakdown.implementation_details: Selection and fabrication of 65 muscles to map to 47 target FACS AUs. Two-stage evaluation: 1) Muscle actuation without skin, 2) Actuation with silicone skin attached.
technical_breakdown.code_complexity: N/A (Hardware-centric paper; computational complexity relates to control algorithms for 65 actuators, not model training)

paper.title: LARF: Learning-aligned Reasoning Framework for Search Relevance
paper.summary: Query-document relevance estimation is a core component of AI-native search systems, where a model must assess whether retrieved documents satisfy users' information needs under complex, multi-dimensional criteria. However, directly applying large language models (LLMs) to this task remains challenging because conventional supervised fine-tuning (SFT) provides limited supervision for domain-specific judgment rationales, while standard trajectory-level reinforcement learning (RL) objectives do not explicitly enforce margin separation among adjacent ordinal relevance labels. Moreover, although such reasoning can be useful during training, chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning is impractical for latency-sensitive online ranking. These challenges make it difficult to resolve ambiguous decision boundaries. We propose a three-stage framework LARF (Learning-Aligned Reasoning Framework for Search Relevance): it first performs cold-start SFT on strategically selected samples with multi-agent guided CoT rationales, then applies discriminative GRPO with attribute-wise, list-wise, and rule-consistency rewards together with a margin loss on the terminal relevance token, and finally distills the teacher into a dual-head student whose classification heads are retained for non-autoregressive inference. On a human-annotated web search relevance benchmark with approximately 300K training and 16K test instances, LARF-8B improves six-class classification accuracy by 5.78 percentage points and NDCG by 5.05 points, while the classification-only serving path reduces inference latency by 82.9\%. These results indicate that aligning structured reasoning, terminal decision optimization, and classification-head distillation can provide an effective accuracy--efficiency trade-off for industrial search relevance modeling.

analysis.problem_statement: The paper addresses the challenge of achieving high-accuracy, domain-specific query-document relevance estimation with LLMs while overcoming the limitations of standard SFT and RL in enforcing ordinal label separation and the latency constraints of chain-of-thought inference in online ranking.
analysis.bottleneck_addressed: Latency-efficiency trade-off in LLM-based inference and the lack of explicit supervision for fine-grained, ordinal decision boundaries in relevance judgment.
analysis.executive_summary: This work bridges the gap between complex reasoning capabilities and the strict latency requirements of industrial search systems by decoupling reasoning from final classification. It demonstrates that a multi-stage training pipeline can significantly enhance relevance accuracy while enabling a non-autoregressive serving path that drastically reduces inference costs.

key_metrics.primary_metric: Six-class classification accuracy and NDCG improvement on a human-annotated web search benchmark
key_metrics.metric_value: +5.78 percentage points in accuracy, +5.05 points in NDCG, 82.9% reduction in inference latency
key_metrics.baseline: Standard LLM fine-tuning baselines (implied comparison to conventional SFT/RL approaches)

technical_breakdown.method: A three-stage framework: (1) Cold-start SFT with multi-agent guided Chain-of-Thought (CoT) rationales; (2) Discrimative Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) using attribute-wise, list-wise, and rule-consistency rewards plus a margin loss on the terminal token; (3) Distillation into a dual-head student model for non-autoregressive inference.
technical_breakdown.architecture: Teacher-student architecture where the teacher generates CoT reasoning and the student retains classification heads for direct, non-autoregressive prediction.
technical_breakdown.implementation_details: Utilizes GRPO with specific reward functions (attribute-wise, list-wise, rule-consistency), applies a margin loss to enforce separation between adjacent ordinal labels, and employs strategic sample selection for SFT.
technical_breakdown.code_complexity: High training complexity due to multi-stage pipeline (SFT + RL + Distillation), but significantly lower inference complexity/latency due to the non-autoregressive classification head serving path.

paper.title: User-Adaptive Fusion of Multiple Foundation Models for Recommender Systems
paper.summary: Can recommender systems benefit from combining a collection of foundation models within and across modalities? While different foundation models may capture complementary aspects of item metadata, we find that naively combining their representations yields only marginal gains over using a single foundation model. We make a key observation: the users who benefit vary across foundation models. Motivated by this observation, we introduce UF2O, a user-adaptive approach for fusing multiple foundation models for recommendation. In a nutshell, UF2O models the contribution of each foundation model as user-specific by maintaining separate recommendation views and adaptively combining their scores for each user. By performing fusion at the score level, UF2O can also fuse heterogeneous foundation models without directly aligning their representation spaces. Extensive experiments that jointly combine four foundation models on four datasets show that UF2O outperforms existing fusion approaches in both static and sequential recommendation settings, with improvements of up to 7% over the strongest fusion baseline. The code, datasets, and supplementary materials for our work are available at https://github.com/kswoo97/UFFO.

analysis.problem_statement: How to effectively fuse multiple heterogeneous foundation models for recommender systems to capture complementary item metadata without suffering from the marginal gains of naive representation combination.
analysis.bottleneck_addressed: Inefficiency of naive ensemble methods in leveraging complementary strengths of diverse foundation models due to user-specific benefit variances and misaligned representation spaces.
analysis.executive_summary: This paper addresses the limitation of combining foundation models in recommendation by demonstrating that naive fusion yields only marginal improvements. It introduces UF2O, a user-adaptive score-level fusion method that allows heterogeneous models to be combined without representation alignment, significantly outperforming existing fusion baselines.

key_metrics.primary_metric: Outperformance over strongest fusion baseline in static and sequential recommendation settings

technical_breakdown.method: User-adaptive fusion at the score level, modeling the contribution of each foundation model as user-specific by maintaining separate recommendation views and adaptively combining their scores.
technical_breakdown.architecture: UF2O framework consisting of multiple foundation model backends, separate recommendation views for each model, and a user-adaptive score combination mechanism.
technical_breakdown.implementation_details: Fusion is performed at the score level rather than the representation level, enabling the integration of heterogeneous foundation models without requiring direct alignment of their latent spaces. The system jointly combines four foundation models across four datasets.
technical_breakdown.code_complexity: Not explicitly stated in the abstract, but implies increased computational overhead due to maintaining and processing multiple separate recommendation views and adaptive score combination logic compared to single-model or naive fusion approaches.

paper.title: Social Interaction Breaks Replicate Independence in Controlled-Clone LLM Agents
paper.summary: Multi-agent LLM evaluations and social simulations create many agents from one model and treat them as independent replicates, even after the agents interact. This assumption remains untested with matched controls. We introduce SocCogEval, a controlled-clone assay for Social Cognitive Transfer (SCT). Clones share the base model, system prompt, and decoding parameters and differ only in a private brief, and a factorial protocol separates the brief, 30 rounds of interaction, and initialization noise. On Qwen3-122B-FP8, interaction with the briefs held fixed raises off-topic BFI-10 response-profile drift by $\barΔ=+0.917$ and $+0.912$ in two topically disjoint scenarios (exact $p=0.0008$ and $0.0039$). The drift is larger than under the brief alone, persists under temperature-zero re-probing, and stays positive without typed memory extraction in exploratory tests. Matched solo generation reproduces part of it, and social interaction remains highest. Across five more model variants, every scenario-averaged interaction contrast is positive. Each interacting population is therefore one replicate, and treating its agents as independent requires paired no-interaction controls.

analysis.problem_statement: The paper addresses the untested statistical assumption that LLM agents derived from the same base model and interacting in a multi-agent setting remain independent replicates, which invalidates standard evaluation metrics.
analysis.bottleneck_addressed: Statistical validity and independence assumptions in multi-agent LLM evaluation and social simulation benchmarks.
analysis.executive_summary: This work demonstrates that social interaction between controlled-clone LLM agents induces significant, persistent behavioral drift that violates the independence assumption required for standard statistical testing. By introducing SocCogEval, the authors provide a controlled-clone assay that quantifies this drift, showing that interacting populations must be treated as single replicates rather than independent samples. This finding necessitates a shift in how multi-agent LLM evaluations are designed and analyzed to avoid false positives and overestimation of model capabilities.

key_metrics.primary_metric: Off-topic BFI-10 response-profile drift (Social Cognitive Transfer)
key_metrics.baseline: Matched solo generation and brief-only controls
key_metrics.improvement_percentage: N/A (Metric represents drift magnitude, not performance improvement)

technical_breakdown.method: A factorial protocol using controlled clones that share base model, system prompt, and decoding parameters, differing only in private briefs, to isolate the effects of interaction, brief content, and initialization noise.
technical_breakdown.architecture: SocCogEval assay framework utilizing Qwen3-122B-FP8 and five other model variants, with a 30-round interaction protocol and temperature-zero re-probing mechanisms.
technical_breakdown.implementation_details: Use of BFI-10 response profiles to measure drift, exact p-value calculation (0.0008 and 0.0039), and exploratory tests without typed memory extraction to verify persistence of drift.
technical_breakdown.code_complexity: N/A (Evaluation framework; computational cost dominated by 30 rounds of interaction across multiple model variants and scenarios)

paper.title: A Description-Derived Drug-Drug Interaction Benchmark Reveals Split-Dependent Molecular Representation Rankings
paper.summary: Drug-drug interaction (DDI) prediction is clinically important and poses a distinct challenge for molecular representation learning. Unlike single-molecule property prediction, DDI requires a predictor to compose two molecular representations into a relational outcome. DrugBank provides curator-authored DDI descriptions rather than ready-made categorical labels, so a categorical prediction target must first be derived from the text. We construct a dataset of DDI pairs by mapping processed descriptions to six text-derived categories and define a benchmark with four holdout regimes that restrict train-test chemical overlap from random pairs to scaffold-disjoint evaluation. We then use this benchmark to compare molecular fingerprints, pretrained sequence representations, and graph-derived features across five seeds and multiple classifier heads. Molecular fingerprints lead the high- overlap random split, whereas graph-derived representations lead the drug- and scaffold-holdout regimes, with the gap increasing as molecular overlap is restricted. Changing the classifier head affects absolute performance but not the relative representation ranking. These results show that representation rankings change with test-set novelty under a fixed description-derived label space.
paper.comment: Accepted at two NeurIPS 2026 workshops: Representations for the Physical Sciences and ML4Molecules

analysis.problem_statement: The paper addresses the lack of standardized, chemically rigorous benchmarks for drug-drug interaction (DDI) prediction that account for molecular novelty and the derivation of categorical labels from unstructured textual descriptions.
analysis.bottleneck_addressed: Evaluation bias in molecular representation learning, specifically the discrepancy between performance on random splits versus scaffold-disjoint splits, and the ambiguity in defining prediction targets from curated text.
analysis.executive_summary: This work establishes a rigorous benchmark for DDI prediction by deriving categorical labels from DrugBank descriptions and defining four holdout regimes that restrict chemical overlap. It reveals that representation rankings are split-dependent, with molecular fingerprints excelling in high-overlap scenarios while graph-derived representations dominate in scaffold-disjoint settings, highlighting the critical importance of test-set novelty in evaluating molecular AI models.

key_metrics.primary_metric: Relative ranking of molecular representations across different chemical overlap regimes
key_metrics.baseline: Molecular fingerprints, pretrained sequence representations, and graph-derived features

technical_breakdown.method: Construction of a DDI dataset by mapping processed DrugBank descriptions to six text-derived categories, followed by comparative evaluation of various molecular representations under four distinct holdout regimes (random to scaffold-disjoint).
technical_breakdown.architecture: Benchmark framework consisting of a label derivation pipeline, four data splitting strategies, and a comparative evaluation harness using multiple classifier heads.
technical_breakdown.implementation_details: Use of DrugBank curator-authored descriptions, mapping to six categories, evaluation across five seeds, and comparison of fingerprints, sequence embeddings, and graph features.
technical_breakdown.code_complexity: N/A (Focus is on benchmark construction and evaluation rather than novel model training complexity)

paper.title: Protective-Design Pre-Emption in Child-Facing Generative AI
paper.summary: Generative AI is adopted rapidly by children, yet unrestricted general-audience models dominate their usage. This paper presents the open problem of \emph{protective-design pre-emption}: Delayed market introduction, low access thresholds, utility gaps, habituation, and peer adoption foster unrestricted AI model lock-in, leading children to bypass child-centric platforms. With first signs of lower adoption of child-centric platforms, we argue that this shift may reinforce existing AI risks such as exposing children to deepened parasocial dependencies, skill erosion, and misinformation. To address this problem, we propose interdisciplinary research directions to quantify pre-emption, understand its socio-technical drivers, and develop interventions ensuring child-centric AI is actively adopted, not just available.
paper.comment: Accepted for NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on Child Safety in AI

analysis.problem_statement: The paper addresses the 'protective-design pre-emption' problem, where unrestricted general-audience AI models lock in children's usage habits before child-centric platforms can gain sufficient adoption, thereby bypassing safety-specific interventions.
analysis.bottleneck_addressed: Socio-technical adoption barriers and market timing gaps that prevent the effective deployment of safety-aligned, child-specific AI systems against dominant general-purpose models.
analysis.executive_summary: This paper highlights a critical gap in AI safety where the rapid adoption of unrestricted generative AI by children outpaces the uptake of specialized, safer alternatives. It argues that this 'pre-emption' leads to increased risks such as parasocial dependencies and misinformation exposure, necessitating a shift from merely providing child-centric AI to actively ensuring its adoption through interdisciplinary interventions.

key_metrics.primary_metric: Quantification of protective-design pre-emption and adoption rates of child-centric vs. general-audience AI
key_metrics.baseline: Current market adoption trends of unrestricted general-audience AI models

technical_breakdown.method: Interdisciplinary analysis of socio-technical drivers (market introduction timing, access thresholds, utility gaps, habituation, and peer adoption) to identify mechanisms of lock-in and propose research directions for intervention.
technical_breakdown.architecture: Conceptual framework for analyzing AI adoption dynamics in pediatric populations; no specific neural network architecture is proposed.
technical_breakdown.implementation_details: Proposes research directions to quantify pre-emption and develop interventions; focuses on policy, design, and social science methodologies rather than algorithmic implementation.

paper.title: ThinkMorph-SSL: Scaling Interleaved Multimodal Reasoning with Pretext Tasks
paper.summary: People reason with pictures as well as words. Interleaved multimodal reasoning gives models a similar way to solve problems by creating intermediate images and using them to guide further reasoning. Training models with this ability usually relies on task-specific demonstrations, which are difficult to collect. We introduce ThinkMorph-SSL, a two-stage training recipe that uses images themselves as a source of supervision. The first stage, pretext reasoning, converts visual pretext tasks, such as image colorization and denoising, into instruction-free interleaved traces. Models describe a corrupted or transformed image, generate a restored or canonical image, and interpret the result. The second stage uses automatically constructed demonstrations for question-driven instruction tuning. At the same instruction-tuning budget, models trained with pretext reasoning outperform those trained with instruction tuning alone. The full recipe improves over the base model by an average of 11.33 accuracy points across twelve benchmarks. These results show that supervision derived from images can build the visual skills needed for interleaved reasoning and improve learning from task-specific demonstrations.

analysis.problem_statement: Training interleaved multimodal reasoning models is hindered by the high cost and difficulty of collecting task-specific demonstrations that include intermediate visual steps.
analysis.bottleneck_addressed: Data scarcity for complex, multi-step visual reasoning tasks requiring intermediate image generation.
analysis.executive_summary: This paper addresses the data bottleneck in training models to reason with both text and images by leveraging self-supervised pretext tasks. By using images themselves as a source of supervision, the method generates instruction-free interleaved traces, reducing reliance on expensive manual annotation. This approach significantly improves reasoning capabilities without increasing the instruction-tuning budget.

key_metrics.primary_metric: Average accuracy improvement across twelve benchmarks

technical_breakdown.method: A two-stage training recipe: Stage 1 uses pretext reasoning to convert visual tasks (colorization, denoising) into interleaved traces; Stage 2 uses automatically constructed demonstrations for question-driven instruction tuning.
technical_breakdown.architecture: Interleaved multimodal reasoning model capable of generating and interpreting intermediate images.
technical_breakdown.implementation_details: Pretext tasks include image colorization and denoising; models describe corrupted images, generate restored images, and interpret results to create instruction-free traces.
technical_breakdown.code_complexity: Not specified in the provided metadata.

paper.title: Unifying Partner and Environment Diversity to Improve Human-AI Coordination
paper.summary: Real-world applications of modern AI systems require generalization to both unseen environments and novel human users. The field of zero-shot coordination (ZSC) has focused primarily on deploying AI to cooperate with novel partners in otherwise familiar environments. Popular population-based methods achieve this by partnering the agent with a diversity of simulated human users during training in a fixed environment, but does not consider the more realistic scenario where both the users and the environment are unseen during training. Recently, training across environments has been explored in training a single self-play agent, which shows better generalization on both novel human users and unseen environments. In this work, we ask whether jointly modeling partner diversity and environment diversity yields stronger coordination with novel partners in novel environments. We introduce Cross Environment Co-Play (CECP), a two-stage framework that first trains a population of self-play agents across a distribution of procedurally generated environments, and then trains a cooperator policy against this partner population. To further couple social and environmental reasoning, we add a next-state prediction module that encourages representations to encode both partner behavior and task structure. We evaluate CECP on both a neuroscience-inspired cooperative foraging task, and the popular ZSC benchmark Overcooked, under held-out partner and held-out environment conditions. CECP achieves the strongest performance among the compared baselines and attains state-of-the-art results under our evaluation protocol for human-AI collaboration. We analyze the model's latent representation encoded by the next-state prediction module, showing it can not only improve the performance of the cooperative AI, but also provide more interpretable latents, demonstrated by the inference of partner skill levels.

analysis.problem_statement: How to enable AI agents to effectively coordinate with novel human partners in previously unseen environments, a scenario where both the partner and the task context are unknown during training.
analysis.bottleneck_addressed: Generalization gap in zero-shot coordination (ZSC) when both the human partner and the environment are novel, moving beyond single-environment or single-partner diversity training.
analysis.executive_summary: This work addresses the critical limitation of current ZSC methods that fail to generalize when both the human user and the environment are unseen. By jointly modeling partner and environment diversity, the proposed framework enhances the robustness of AI cooperation in realistic, dynamic scenarios. This is significant for deploying AI systems in real-world applications where fixed training environments do not reflect the variability of actual deployment conditions.

key_metrics.primary_metric: Strongest performance among compared baselines and state-of-the-art results under held-out partner and environment conditions.
key_metrics.baseline: Population-based methods in fixed environments and single self-play agents trained across environments.

technical_breakdown.method: Cross Environment Co-Play (CECP), a two-stage framework that first trains a population of self-play agents across procedurally generated environments, then trains a cooperator policy against this diverse partner population.
technical_breakdown.architecture: Includes a cooperator policy and a next-state prediction module designed to couple social and environmental reasoning by encoding both partner behavior and task structure.
technical_breakdown.implementation_details: Uses procedurally generated environments for training diversity; employs a next-state prediction module to improve latent representation interpretability and performance.
technical_breakdown.code_complexity: Not specified in abstract; likely involves significant computational overhead due to training across a distribution of environments and maintaining a population of agents.

paper.title: How Much Dependency Can a Marginal Rule See? Total Correlation in Diffusion LM Parallel Decoding
paper.summary: A masked diffusion language model is fast because it commits several tokens per step. Each token is sampled from its own marginal, so the dependency between the tokens is lost, and the size of that loss is the conditional total correlation C of the committed set. Most decoders choose the set from per-position marginals, which can bound C but cannot determine it. We ask how well they predict it. We estimate C for fixed candidate sets on four masked diffusion LMs from two families. On three of the four, the best marginal-only predictor is off by about one bit (0.74 to 1.17), 1.8 to 3.7 times less than a baseline that knows only the bound, and most of this accuracy comes from the bound itself. On a subset, our estimate ranks sets like the exact KL cost of a parallel commit, but sits a median 0.4 to 1.1 bits below it on prose and when the rest of the text is still masked. Dream-instruct is the exception, mainly on prose, where its conditionals are least self-consistent. Among six common marginal rules, pooling over the set beats gating on its weakest position in all 24 paired comparisons. The measurement needs a validated readout: Dream and LLaDA place a position's prediction at different logit indices, and the wrong index inflates an inconsistency diagnostic 14 to 41 times. We give three checks that measure the convention. Our results concern predicting C for a fixed set, not what a dependency-aware decoder gains.
paper.comment: NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on Diffusion Language Models: Foundations, Efficiency, and Reasoning (DiffuLM). Code: https://github.com/DovudAsadov/dllm-total-correlation

analysis.problem_statement: The paper investigates the accuracy of marginal-only predictors in estimating the conditional total correlation (dependency loss) inherent in parallel decoding steps of masked diffusion language models.
analysis.bottleneck_addressed: Inefficiency and quality degradation in parallel decoding due to the loss of inter-token dependencies when sampling from independent marginals.
analysis.executive_summary: This work quantifies the 'dependency loss' in diffusion LMs, showing that standard marginal-based decoders significantly underestimate the true cost of parallel commits. It reveals that while marginal rules can predict this loss better than simple bounds, they still exhibit substantial error margins, highlighting a critical gap in current decoding strategies for efficient diffusion models.

key_metrics.primary_metric: Prediction error of conditional total correlation (C) by marginal-only predictors
key_metrics.baseline: Baseline that knows only the bound on C
key_metrics.improvement_percentage: 1.8 to 3.7 times less error than the bound-only baseline

technical_breakdown.method: Estimates conditional total correlation for fixed candidate token sets and compares these estimates against predictions derived solely from per-position marginals.
technical_breakdown.architecture: Evaluated on four masked diffusion LMs from two families, specifically analyzing the readout conventions of models like Dream-instruct and LLaDA.
technical_breakdown.implementation_details: Utilizes a validated readout to measure inconsistency diagnostics, comparing six common marginal rules (e.g., pooling vs. gating) and identifying that incorrect logit index placement can inflate diagnostics by 14 to 41 times.
technical_breakdown.code_complexity: Not specified in summary; focuses on measurement and prediction accuracy rather than training complexity.

paper.title: Compressible Representations: Functional Spines in Deep Neural Networks
paper.summary: Deep networks embed inputs in high-dimensional representations, but how much of this capacity actually drives behavior? We introduce a framework for identifying, at each layer, the subspace of the representation that is functionally sensitive to the task. Using a matrix analogous to the Fisher information but defined over the hidden representation, we rank directions by their influence on downstream computation and project onto the most task-sensitive subspace. Across pretrained vision networks, representations are remarkably compressible: a small fraction of the task-sensitive subspace preserves most performance, often requiring far fewer dimensions than geometric alternatives. We find that this compressed representation is also more robust to adversarial attacks generated on the full network. We additionally show that this decomposition recovers functionally distinct subspaces within the same representation: on cue-conflict stimuli, shape-sensitive and texture-sensitive directions are largely non-overlapping, and ablating one selectively impairs the corresponding task while leaving the other intact. Task-sensitive subspaces also provide a principled foundation for continual learning: constraining gradient updates to lie orthogonal to the task-sensitive subspaces of prior tasks outperforms standard variance-based gradient projection methods. Finally, restricting representational comparisons to task-sensitive subspaces reveals that inter-model alignment is higher in task-sensitive directions than in task-insensitive directions at later layers, and that conditioning on different tasks over the same stimuli uncovers asymmetries that full-space similarity measures cannot detect. Together, these results establish that deep networks compute through a low-dimensional functional spine embedded within a much larger representational space.

analysis.problem_statement: Determining the minimal subspace of high-dimensional deep network representations that is functionally necessary for task performance and robustness.
analysis.bottleneck_addressed: Inefficiency and redundancy in high-dimensional representational spaces, leading to unnecessary computational costs and vulnerability to adversarial perturbations.
analysis.executive_summary: This paper introduces a method to identify a 'functional spine' in deep networks, showing that task performance relies on a low-dimensional subspace rather than the full representation. This finding enables significant model compression, improved adversarial robustness, and more effective continual learning by focusing on functionally sensitive directions.

technical_breakdown.method: Uses a matrix analogous to Fisher information defined over hidden representations to rank directions by influence on downstream computation, then projects onto the most task-sensitive subspace.
technical_breakdown.architecture: Applicable to pretrained vision networks; operates on hidden layer representations.
technical_breakdown.implementation_details: Ranks representation directions via a task-sensitivity metric; projects onto the top-k sensitive subspace; uses orthogonal gradient projection for continual learning; analyzes cue-conflict stimuli to disentangle shape vs. texture sensitivity.
technical_breakdown.code_complexity: Requires computation of a representation-level sensitivity matrix; projection and gradient constraints add overhead but reduce effective dimensionality for downstream tasks.

paper.title: RoMo Hands: A Large Scale Richly Organized Text to Hand Motion Dataset
paper.summary: While text-driven body motion generation has matured, pure-hand synthesis remains bottlenecked by data. Existing datasets often treat hands as rigid end-effectors, lack fine-grained captions, or are too limited in scale to support robust generalization. We introduce RoMo Hands, an in-the-wild, text-paired dataset of ~542K sequences (884 hours, 95.5M frames at 30 fps) which is an order of magnitude larger than prior work. To ensure high-quality supervision, a stringent dexterity filter discards low-articulation sequences, focusing the distribution on complex bimanual movement. Each clip is paired with five captions at increasing granularities from global semantic tags to atomic finger states, organized under a hierarchical taxonomy. To bridge the gap between body and hand architectures, we propose a novel 393-D bimanual representation that adapts redundant body-motion paradigms to the high-DoF kinematics of hands. Systematic benchmarking of diffusion, masked-token, and autoregressive generators reveals distinct trade-offs under these hand-specific adaptations, including a sharp divergence between semantic alignment and kinematic plausibility. Our dataset, representation, and benchmark establish a rigorous foundation for the next generation of dexterous motion synthesis. Project page: https://romodataset.github.io/romo-hands/.
paper.comment: Accepted to NeurIPS 2026. Project page: https://romodataset.github.io/romo-hands/ Dataset: https://huggingface.co/datasets/RoMoDataset/RoMo-Hands

analysis.problem_statement: Pure-hand motion synthesis is hindered by the lack of large-scale, high-quality datasets with fine-grained textual supervision and appropriate high-degree-of-freedom kinematic representations.
analysis.bottleneck_addressed: Data scarcity and quality for fine-grained dexterous hand motion generation.
analysis.executive_summary: This paper addresses the critical data bottleneck in text-to-hand motion generation by introducing RoMo Hands, a dataset 10x larger than prior work with hierarchical captions. It also proposes a novel 393-D bimanual representation to adapt body-motion architectures to the complex kinematics of hands, establishing a rigorous benchmark for future dexterous synthesis.

technical_breakdown.method: The paper introduces a large-scale in-the-wild dataset filtered by a dexterity metric to ensure complex bimanual movement, paired with a hierarchical taxonomy of captions. It defines a 393-D bimanual representation to bridge body and hand architectures and benchmarks diffusion, masked-token, and autoregressive models.
technical_breakdown.architecture: Bimanual kinematic representation (393-D), hierarchical captioning taxonomy, and comparative benchmarking of diffusion, masked-token, and autoregressive generators.
technical_breakdown.implementation_details: Stringent dexterity filter to discard low-articulation sequences; five levels of caption granularity from global semantic tags to atomic finger states; adaptation of redundant body-motion paradigms to high-DoF hand kinematics.
technical_breakdown.code_complexity: Not specified in the abstract; implies high computational cost due to the large scale (95.5M frames) and high-dimensional representation (393-D).

paper.title: Tokenization and Architecture Jointly Allocate Component Roles in Time Series Transformers
paper.summary: Time series transformers have achieved strong forecasting performance, yet it remains unclear which of their components, attention or the feed-forward network (FFN), constructs temporal features, and how tokenization such as patching changes this. We propose a temporal probing framework that uses 15 token-level diagnostic tasks to measure feature construction as the gain in linear decodability of temporal properties from one sub-layer to the next (a matched MLP probe already saturates at the embedding). It targets models whose probed representations are read by a linear forecasting head. Applied to 5 supervised models trained on 8 long-term forecasting benchmarks, it finds that the constructing component is not fixed but allocated by the interaction of tokenization and architecture. Under patch tokenization (PatchTST), the FFN's gain exceeds attention's in probing on all 8 datasets, and its 8-dataset mean is 3.2x attention's. Without attention, the FFN alone reaches nearly the same total gain, both when attention is removed from a trained model and when PatchTST is trained without it, and the retrained model forecasts within a few percent of the full model. In probing, attention dominates under variate tokenization (iTransformer); in CATS, cross-attention is the only input path. In a controlled manipulation of PatchTST, single-scalar tokens (P=1) nearly eliminate the FFN's construction, while one more point per token (P=2) restores it. Our forecasting-side interventions (activation patching, knockout, and training without attention) establish component-level reliance and sufficiency. These results offer a representational reading of prior findings on the gains from patching, the competitiveness of self-attention-free models (TSMixer, PatchMLP), and the distinct role of cross-attention in CATS.
paper.comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026. 42 pages, 3 figures. Code: https://github.com/mingyu-11/tokenization-component-roles

analysis.problem_statement: The paper addresses the lack of clarity regarding which specific components of time series transformers (attention vs. feed-forward networks) construct temporal features and how tokenization strategies alter this functional allocation.
analysis.bottleneck_addressed: Interpretability and mechanistic understanding of neural network components in time series forecasting models.
analysis.executive_summary: This work provides a causal and representational analysis of time series transformers, revealing that the role of attention versus FFNs is not fixed but depends on the interaction between tokenization and architecture. It demonstrates that under patch tokenization, FFNs are the primary constructors of temporal features, while attention dominates under variate tokenization, offering a theoretical explanation for the success of attention-free models like TSMixer and PatchMLP.

key_metrics.primary_metric: Gain in linear decodability of temporal properties (probing accuracy) attributed to specific components
key_metrics.metric_value: FFN gain is 3.2x attention's mean gain under PatchTST
key_metrics.baseline: Attention mechanism vs. Feed-Forward Network (FFN) contributions

technical_breakdown.method: A temporal probing framework using 15 token-level diagnostic tasks to measure feature construction as the gain in linear decodability from one sub-layer to the next, combined with forecasting-side interventions like activation patching and knockout experiments.
technical_breakdown.architecture: Analyzes PatchTST, iTransformer, and CATS architectures, focusing on the interaction between tokenization (patch vs. variate vs. scalar) and internal components (self-attention, cross-attention, FFN).
technical_breakdown.implementation_details: Uses matched MLP probes to establish baselines, linear probing for decodability, and controlled manipulations such as removing attention or changing patch size (P=1 vs P=2) to isolate component roles.
technical_breakdown.code_complexity: Requires training multiple supervised models on 8 long-term forecasting benchmarks and extensive probing/intervention experiments; computational cost is moderate to high due to the need for retraining models without attention and running multiple diagnostic tasks.

paper.title: Localizing Cross-Lingual Generalization in Parameter Space
paper.summary: Cross-lingual transfer is uneven across tasks, succeeding for natural language understanding but often failing for mathematical reasoning. We argue that this asymmetry is governed by the geometry of parameter space. Specifically, cross-lingual generalization is determined by whether English and target-language LoRA adapters share a low-error basin. To test this, we use linear mode connectivity (LMC) between English and target-language adapters, evaluating on three tasks. We find that NLI and QA model-language pairs are mostly linearly connected, whereas mathematical reasoning (Math) pairs are not, indicating that basin geometry is task-dependent. Such disconnection in Math is ``local'' rather than global. A small target-language task sample, applied only to the English adapter's language encoding or semantic composition layers, is enough to repair it. Cross-lingual generalization is also factorizable into language-specific encoding and language-agnostic composition, each supplied separately from a cheaper signal. English task data routed to the composition layers and an unlabeled target-language corpus routed to the language encoding layers each alleviate it on their own for nearly every pair. Composition is the more influential of these, and it needs no target-language data. Together, these results suggest that cross-lingual generalization decomposes into language-specific and language-agnostic components in parameter space. This decomposition offers a practical route for low-resource cross-lingual adaptation.

analysis.problem_statement: The paper addresses the inconsistent success of cross-lingual transfer, specifically why it works for natural language understanding tasks but often fails for mathematical reasoning.
analysis.bottleneck_addressed: Cross-lingual generalization asymmetry and the high data cost of adapting models to low-resource languages.
analysis.executive_summary: This work identifies that the failure of cross-lingual transfer in mathematical reasoning is due to a lack of linear mode connectivity between English and target-language LoRA adapters, unlike in NLI/QA tasks. It demonstrates that this disconnection is local and can be repaired by fine-tuning specific layers (language encoding or semantic composition) with minimal data. The findings provide a practical, low-cost strategy for cross-lingual adaptation by decoupling language-specific encoding from language-agnostic composition.

key_metrics.primary_metric: Linear Mode Connectivity (LMC) between English and target-language LoRA adapters
key_metrics.metric_value: Qualitative: NLI/QA pairs are mostly linearly connected; Math pairs are not.
key_metrics.baseline: Standard cross-lingual transfer without targeted layer-specific fine-tuning.
key_metrics.improvement_percentage: Not quantified in the abstract; improvement is described as 'alleviating' disconnection and enabling generalization.

technical_breakdown.method: Uses Linear Mode Connectivity (LMC) to analyze the geometry of parameter space for LoRA adapters. Repairs cross-lingual disconnection by applying small target-language task samples to specific layers (language encoding or semantic composition) of the English adapter.
technical_breakdown.architecture: LoRA adapters for English and target languages; decomposition into language-specific encoding layers and language-agnostic semantic composition layers.
technical_breakdown.implementation_details: Evaluation on three tasks (NLI, QA, Math). Targeted fine-tuning of either language encoding layers (using unlabeled target-language corpus) or composition layers (using English task data).
technical_breakdown.code_complexity: Low computational overhead for repair, as it requires only a small target-language task sample and targeted layer updates rather than full model retraining.

paper.title: Faithful Persona Steering under Incongruity via Dual-Stream Refinement
paper.summary: Standard LLM personalization typically frames identity as a static retrieval task, overlooking the inherent incongruity of human personas, where stable traits coexist with atypical, context-specific stances. Existing methods struggle to reconcile these dimensions: prompting succumbs to context drift over long sequences, while fine-tuning often suppresses idiosyncratic "quirks" in favor of generic distributional patterns. To bridge this gap, we present QuirkyMind, a framework that disentangles identity definition from its expression. First, Traits Anchoring constructs a dual-stream latent state, fusing a sentence-level summary for semantic stability with a token-level sequence for generative control. This state is stabilized via In-Context Narrative Refinement using an alternating objective: a discriminative InfoNCE loss anchors the persona in representation space to prevent drift, while a generative cross-entropy loss ensures faithful verbalization. Finally, Persona Steered Generalization transfers the refined state to downstream tasks via parameter-efficient adapters. Empirical evaluations on Persona-Steered QA and Narrative Inference demonstrate that QuirkyMind mitigates drift, consolidating persona knowledge without erasing authentic incongruities.
paper.comment: Accepted to Findings of ACL 2026. 18 pages, 14 figures, 8 tables

analysis.problem_statement: Standard LLM personalization methods fail to maintain consistent, idiosyncratic human personas over long sequences, often suppressing unique traits in favor of generic patterns or suffering from context drift.
analysis.bottleneck_addressed: Long-context consistency and faithful persona retention in Large Language Models.
analysis.executive_summary: This paper addresses the critical limitation of current personalization techniques that treat identity as static retrieval, leading to the loss of authentic, context-specific 'quirks' in LLMs. By disentangling identity definition from expression, the proposed framework ensures that stable traits are maintained without erasing the incongruities that define a unique persona, which is essential for realistic and reliable role-playing applications.

key_metrics.primary_metric: Mitigation of persona drift and consolidation of persona knowledge while preserving authentic incongruities.

technical_breakdown.method: The framework, QuirkyMind, uses a dual-stream latent state to separate semantic stability from generative control, stabilized by an alternating objective function that combines discriminative and generative losses.
technical_breakdown.architecture: Dual-stream latent state (sentence-level summary + token-level sequence), In-Context Narrative Refinement module, and parameter-efficient adapters for downstream task transfer.
technical_breakdown.implementation_details: Uses InfoNCE loss for discriminative anchoring in representation space to prevent drift, and cross-entropy loss for generative faithful verbalization. Empirical evaluation on Persona-Steered QA and Narrative Inference tasks.
technical_breakdown.code_complexity: Not specified in abstract, but involves dual-stream processing and alternating optimization objectives.

paper.title: SPARQL-Planned Single-Hop Traversal over a Live Knowledge Graph for Multi-Hop Question Answering
paper.summary: Semantic retrieval struggles with multi-hop question answering on both recall and precision: gold passages are buried among distractors that degrade the reader's answer, and retrieving them requires reasoning over the query rather than matching it. GraphRAG techniques expand semantic retrieval by connecting passages to graph nodes and performing one or more hops of expansion after initial retrieval. This improves recall, but multi-hop expansion becomes expensive and brings additional noise into the retrieved set. We break this tradeoff by \emph{interleaving} dense retrieval with knowledge-graph traversal for complex multi-hop questions. Dense retrieval locates the first relevant regions of the search space at good recall, while traversal of a pre-existing external KG (Wikidata) restores precision and improves recall by confirming retrieved passages against a reasoning path through the KG. To keep traversal both question-adaptive and reliable, we have an LLM plan it as code generation task for graph traversal in SPARQL format but \emph{parse rather than execute} the query. On full 1{,}000-question splits under a shared corpus and reader, and with a single configuration applied identically to every dataset, we reach \textbf{62.5 / 75.1} EM/F1 on HotpotQA, \textbf{73.5 / 81.0} on 2WikiMultiHopQA, and \textbf{37.1 / 50.0} on MuSiQue, ahead of reproduced HippoRAG2, T\textsuperscript{2}RAG, and IRCoT on all three benchmarks. A second, token-matched setting stays ahead of T\textsuperscript{2}RAG on HotpotQA and 2Wiki while spending roughly its per-query budget. Executing the generated SPARQL instead of parsing it costs up to 11.4 EM, mostly because raw queries return empty results, not because of syntax errors.

analysis.problem_statement: The paper addresses the tradeoff in multi-hop question answering where semantic retrieval suffers from low recall due to buried gold passages, while graph-based expansion methods introduce high computational costs and noise.
analysis.bottleneck_addressed: Retrieval precision and recall degradation in multi-hop reasoning tasks, specifically the inefficiency and noise introduced by multi-hop graph expansion in GraphRAG systems.
analysis.executive_summary: This work introduces a hybrid approach that interleaves dense retrieval with knowledge-graph traversal to balance recall and precision in multi-hop QA. By using an LLM to plan SPARQL queries that are parsed rather than executed, the method leverages the structure of external knowledge graphs (Wikidata) to confirm retrieved passages without incurring the high costs or empty-result risks of direct query execution.

key_metrics.primary_metric: Exact Match (EM) and F1 score on HotpotQA, 2WikiMultiHopQA, and MuSiQue benchmarks
key_metrics.metric_value: 62.5 EM / 75.1 F1 on HotpotQA; 73.5 EM / 81.0 F1 on 2WikiMultiHopQA; 37.1 EM / 50.0 F1 on MuSiQue
key_metrics.improvement_percentage: Not explicitly quantified as a single percentage, but reported to be ahead of all listed baselines on all three benchmarks.

technical_breakdown.method: The system interleaves dense retrieval with knowledge-graph traversal. An LLM generates a SPARQL query to plan the traversal, which is then parsed (not executed) to guide the retrieval process, allowing the system to confirm passages against a reasoning path in Wikidata.
technical_breakdown.architecture: Components include a dense retriever for initial passage localization, an LLM for code generation (SPARQL planning), a parser for the generated queries, and an external knowledge graph (Wikidata) for traversal and verification.
technical_breakdown.implementation_details: The key technique is 'parsing rather than executing' the LLM-generated SPARQL queries. This avoids the 11.4 EM drop observed when executing raw queries, which often return empty results. The method uses a single configuration applied identically across datasets.
technical_breakdown.code_complexity: The approach reduces the expense of multi-hop expansion by avoiding full graph traversal execution. It maintains a per-query budget comparable to T2RAG in token-matched settings, suggesting efficient computational usage relative to exhaustive graph search.

paper.title: fork() for Agents: Agent Kernel for Non-blocking LLM Orchestration
paper.summary: LLM-based agents typically execute tool calls synchronously and discard completed work upon failure. Subgraph-selective recovery, re-executing only a failed node's transitive descendants, is a well-established pattern in distributed systems (Spark, Erlang/OTP, Dryad), and recent agent runtimes (Sherlock, AgentGit, Atomix) preserve completed work through verifiers, version control, or transactional tool boundaries. We present \textbf{Agent-Kernel}, a non-blocking runtime that ports this pattern to the LLM \emph{content plane}: its primitive, \textbf{Sub-Graph Recovery (SGR)}, fires on a raw exception with no trained verifier or planner, resets a failed node's descendants while preserving completed siblings, and composes each parent's text into its children's prompts (context inheritance), all on a durable substrate with a formal state-preservation guarantee. Across 14{,}434 runs on synthetic and standard benchmarks (tau-bench, Gaia2, AutomationBench, InterruptBench), SGR reaches full recovery within budget=3 where whole-trajectory replay exhausts (100\% vs.\ 55\%), and is roughly 10$\times$ faster than an adapted Sherlock rollback that also recovers. It matches ReAct-serial accuracy within noise on linear workloads while adding recovery and parallelism (up to 12.7$\times$ speedup) where structure permits. Ablation isolates SGR: removing it collapses success to 39.4\%.

analysis.problem_statement: LLM-based agents typically execute tool calls synchronously and discard all completed work upon a single failure, leading to inefficient recovery and wasted computational resources.
analysis.bottleneck_addressed: Inefficient error recovery and lack of parallelism in LLM agent orchestration.
analysis.executive_summary: This paper introduces Agent-Kernel, a non-blocking runtime that enables subgraph-selective recovery for LLM agents, allowing them to preserve completed work and re-execute only failed branches. By porting distributed systems patterns to the LLM content plane, it significantly improves recovery rates and speed compared to whole-trajectory replay or existing agent runtimes.

technical_breakdown.method: Sub-Graph Recovery (SGR) fires on raw exceptions, resets only the failed node's transitive descendants while preserving completed siblings, and composes parent text into children's prompts for context inheritance.
technical_breakdown.architecture: Non-blocking runtime with a durable substrate, formal state-preservation guarantee, and context inheritance mechanism.
technical_breakdown.implementation_details: Uses SGR primitive that requires no trained verifier or planner; composes parent text into children's prompts; operates on a durable substrate.
technical_breakdown.code_complexity: Approximately 10x faster than adapted Sherlock rollback; up to 12.7x speedup where structure permits parallelism.
